newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech budget surplus not tied to bill sale - FinMin.
newsitem.headline: Czech budget surplus not tied to bill sale - FinMin.

text.p: The Czech finance ministry on Monday rejected a local newspaper report which said the country showed a 1996 budget surplus because it counted funds from a late treasury bill issue as revenue.

The daily Mlada Fronta Dnes quoted a central bank source on Friday as saying that the ministry sold three billion crowns in treasury bills in late December, then used the funds to be able to claim a 419 million crown surplus in the 1996 state budget.

Finance Ministry spokeswoman Ludmilla Nutilova told Reuters that the ministry did not claim funds from the 12-month treasury bill sale as a revenue item on the 1996 budget as Mlada Fronta had reported.
"The issuing of T-bills is a standard measure, and it in no way influences the state budget's deficit," Nutilova said.
"The last T-bill was issued for January 2, which means doubts whether it influenced the state (of the budget) in the last year are absolutely uneven," she said.

Finance Ministry officials said on Thursday that 1996 revenue totalled 482.8 billion crowns while expenditure was 482.4 billion crowns, leaving a surplus of roughly 419 million crowns, when a deficit was widely expected.
Nutilova declined to elaborate on how the final budget numbers were determined, but Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik is scheduled to discuss details at a news conference on Tuesday.
It would be the fourth straight year where the country has posted a budget surplus. The government's balanced 1997 budget totalling 549.1 billion crowns was approved last month.

In the autumn, the government made across-the-board spending cuts to avoid a forecast 9.3 billion crown shortfall, caused by higher-than-expected spending, slow repayments from credits extended to Russia, and lower-than-expected tax revenue.

The government then froze selective spending in December, and combined with early payments on credit due from non-budget government agencies, forecast a deficit of 1.2 billion crowns, instead of the more than five billion crown shortfall it feared before the moves were taken.
The 1996 budget was originally approved as a balanced budget totalling 497 billion crowns, but the autumn spending cuts knocked the forecast expenditure down to 491 billion crowns.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus hailed the surplus as a victory, but analysts questioned what bookkeeping manuevers were made to achieve the result.
